questions.cardText:
[Physiology and Anatomy] Which of the following is true about the human brain?
A. The brain can feel pain directly
B. The brain itself doesn’t feel pain
C. The brain is the most sensitive organ to pain
Answer: B. The brain does not have pain receptors and therefore does not feel pain. This is why neurosurgeons can perform brain surgery on conscious patients, allowing them to monitor brain functions like speech and movement during the procedure, reducing the risk of damage to critical areas.
questions.de: Warum spürt das Hirngewebe selbst keinen Schmerz, sodass Neurochirurgen wache Patienten operieren und dabei Sprache und Bewegung überwachen können?
questions.en: Why does brain tissue itself feel no pain, so that neurosurgeons can operate on conscious patients and monitor their speech and movement during surgery?

timeline.labelEn: Wilder Penfield founds the Montreal Neurological Institute, home of his surgery on awake patients under local anaesthesia
timeline.labelDe: Wilder Penfield gründet das Montreal Neurological Institute, wo er wache Patienten unter örtlicher Betäubung am Gehirn operiert

questions.notes: Accept 'no nociceptors'. The brain tissue lacks pain receptors; the scalp, skull lining and meninges do have them, hence local anaesthesia in awake craniotomy. Timeline: Penfield's founding of the MNI (Wilder Penfield article).

questions.cardText:
[Astronomy] How would you weigh on Mars relative to Earth?
A. The same as on Earth
B. More than on Earth
C. Less than on Earth
Answer: C.
questions.de: Wie viel Prozent deines Gewichts auf der Erde würdest du auf dem Mars ungefähr wiegen?
questions.en: Roughly what percentage of your Earth weight would you weigh on Mars?

timeline.labelEn: Asaph Hall discovers Phobos and Deimos, whose orbits first let astronomers estimate the mass of Mars
timeline.labelDe: Asaph Hall entdeckt Phobos und Deimos, deren Bahnen erstmals eine Schätzung der Masse des Mars erlauben

questions.notes: Card answer 'less than on Earth' is right; surface gravity 3.721 m/s², about 38% of Earth's (accept 37–38% or about a third / 0.38 g).
